newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban signal tougher line on drug trade.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban signal tougher line on drug trade.

text.p: A U.N. anti-drug official flew to Taleban headquarters in Kandahar on Sunday to explore how far Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban are willing to crack down on the lucrative narcotics trade in their territory.

"In the past it was extremely difficult for us to operate in Afghanistan since we had to deal with five factions," Giovanni Quaglia, director of the U.N. International Drug Control Programme (UNDCP), told Reuters before leaving Islamabad.
"I will really say our best options are an increased sense of responsibility from the Taleban," he said.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, now control about two-thirds of Afghanistan, including its richest opium poppy-growing areas and smuggling routes to Pakistan, Iran and the Central Asian republic of Turkmenistan.
War-ravaged Afghanistan has become a leading world producer of opium, from which heroin is derived, and some Western nations worry that the Taleban may do little to curb the drug trade.

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, in a report obtained by Reuters, said the Taleban had "reached de facto agreements with the cultivators and perhaps even traffickers to limit their attack on opium cultivation and domestic drug abuse".

In the past the Taleban militants, bent on imposing a harsh version of Islamic sharia law on Afghanistan, have given mixed signals on drugs. They have banned drug abuse and trafficking, and prohibited cultivation of marijuana, but not of opium, on which many Afghan farmers now depend for a livelihood.

The movement's chief Mullah Mohammad Omar said last month that the Taleban, whose leaders are graduates of Islamic seminaries for Afghan refugees in Pakistan, opposed the drug trade, but could not immediately ban opium-growing.
"We have already ordered that there should be no hashish in the country and have destroyed several heroin factories in Spin Boldak and Chattu (near the Pakistani border)," he said.

He said he had ordered the Taleban to stop large-scale movement of opium on main roads, but added: "We cannot stop opium-growing now, though we are against it. We must go step by step because the people are poor and they need an alternative."
The Taleban may not feel able to ban opium-growing, but they are keen to show their hostility to drug trafficking.

On Friday the Taleban said they had seized 14 kg (30 lb) of heroin from Delhi-bound Afghan passengers at Jalalabad airport in the first major drug haul announced by the Islamic zealots since they captured Jalalabad on September 11.
Mullah Alladad, the Taleban commander at the airport, quoted one of the alleged drug couriers as saying the heroin had been brought from Pakistan's tribal area bordering Afghanistan.
Iran has accused the Taleban of fostering the drugs trade on its frontier in western Afghanistan, a charge the Taleban deny.
The Taleban police chief in the western city of Herat told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) last week that a campaign had been launched against heroin and other drugs.

The 28-year-old police chief, Abdul Haq, said 250 to 300 Taleban fighters were patrolling the Iranian border to combat drug smuggling and had seized "thousands of kilograms of opium and a large quantity of heroin" that had later been burned.
He said addicts were being detained for correction. "They are told Islam's point of view on drugs, its negative effects, and are urged to offer prayers and pursue family life," he said.
He showed AIP a 35-year-old addict named Muhammad Zahir who looked pale and weak from his three-year-old habit.
Zahir, a day labourer, said he spent his earnings on heroin and his family, who were always trying to persuade him to stop taking drugs. "I want to give up the habit," he said.
Haq said Zahir would be freed on probation after two to three weeks. If he relapsed he would be sent to court.
Quaglia said the Taleban's rise to power over the past two years had made little difference to Afghanistan's opium output, which rose slightly this year to about 2,300 tonnes.

About 1,000 tonnes are consumed in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Iran, while drug law enforcers seize about 300 tonnes, leaving about 1,000 tonnes to be converted into morphine and heroin for the European and North American markets, he said.
"We do hope that in future, since the Taleban control most of the country, they will take responsibility as well," Quaglia said, adding that it was also vital to dampen demand for drugs.
"Reduction in supply from Afghanistan is very much linked with reduction in demand," he said.
